def: The federal government's budget year. It runs from October 1 to September 30 and is named for the calendar year in which it ends, so FY2026 ran from October 1, 2025, to September 30, 2026.
The amount by which the government's spending exceeds its revenue in a single year. The government covers it by borrowing, which adds to the debt.
The amount by which revenue exceeds spending in a year. The federal government last ran a surplus in fiscal year 2001.

A deficit that persists even when the economy is healthy, because current laws commit the government to spend more than its tax laws collect. It differs from a temporary deficit caused by a recession or an emergency.
Everything the U.S. Treasury owes: debt held by the public plus debt held by federal trust funds and other government accounts. The Treasury publishes it daily as "Debt to the Penny."

Treasury securities owned by investors outside the federal government, including individuals, companies, state and local governments, foreign governments, and the Federal Reserve. Economists consider it the most meaningful measure of debt.

Treasury securities held by federal trust funds and accounts, such as the Social Security and Medicare trust funds and civil service and military retirement funds. It is money one part of the government owes another.
A cap, set in law, on how much the Treasury may borrow. Raising or suspending it doesn't authorize new spending; it lets the Treasury pay for spending and tax laws Congress already passed.
Interest the government pays on debt held by the public, minus interest it receives (for example on student loans and its own cash). It is the cost of past borrowing, not a program.

The Treasury's gross interest cost on all federal debt, including interest credited to trust funds. Because trust fund interest is paid from one government account to another, the budget counts only net interest.

Spending set by permanent law rather than annual votes, mostly for benefit programs like Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid. Anyone who qualifies receives benefits, so costs change automatically with the number of people eligible and the cost of services. Also called direct spending.
A program that legally guarantees benefits to everyone who meets its eligibility rules, such as Social Security or Medicare. Most mandatory spending is for entitlements.

Spending Congress decides on each year in appropriations bills. It pays for the military, and for most of what agencies do, such as education grants, highways, scientific research, national parks, and foreign aid.

Laws that give agencies legal authority to spend money. Congress is supposed to pass 12 regular appropriations bills each year, one for each of its appropriations subcommittees, before the fiscal year starts on October 1.
A stopgap law that keeps agencies funded, usually at the previous year's levels, when Congress hasn't finished its regular appropriations bills. CRs can last days, months, or a full year.
A single huge bill that combines several or all of the 12 regular appropriations bills, often with unrelated provisions attached. A smaller package of a few bills is sometimes called a minibus.

What happens when appropriations lapse: agencies without funding must stop work that isn't legally exempt or essential to protect life and property. Mandatory programs such as Social Security keep paying benefits.
Extra funding passed outside the regular annual bills, usually for emergencies such as disasters, wars, or pandemics. Spending designated as an emergency is typically exempt from budget limits.

Congress's own budget plan, setting overall levels of spending, revenue, and deficits. It is adopted by the House and Senate but not signed by the President, so it is not law. It is required to use reconciliation.

A fast-track process, set up by the Congressional Budget Act of 1974, that lets Congress change taxes, mandatory spending, and the debt limit with a simple majority in the Senate, avoiding a filibuster. It has been used for major tax laws in 2001, 2017, and 2025 and for the American Rescue Plan in 2021.

Rules requiring that new tax cuts or mandatory spending be offset so they don't increase deficits. The Statutory PAYGO Act of 2010 enforces this with automatic cuts, but Congress has routinely waived it.
Automatic, across-the-board spending cuts triggered when Congress exceeds spending caps or PAYGO limits, as under the Budget Control Act of 2011.

CBO's projection of spending, revenue, and deficits for the next ten years if current laws stay the same. It is a benchmark for measuring the cost of proposed legislation, not a forecast of what Congress will do.
A nonpartisan agency of Congress, created in 1974, that projects the budget and economy and estimates the cost of legislation. It makes no policy recommendations.
A nonpartisan committee of Congress whose staff estimate the revenue effects of tax legislation. CBO uses JCT's estimates for tax provisions.
The White House office that prepares the President's budget request and oversees how agencies spend money.
The U.S. Treasury's official monthly report of federal receipts, outlays, and the deficit or surplus. The September edition gives final totals for the fiscal year.
Money the government actually pays out in a given period, such as benefit checks, salaries, and payments to contractors. It differs from budget authority, which is the legal permission to spend.
Payments minus offsetting collections and receipts, such as Medicare premiums, fees, and loan repayments. This is how the Treasury reports spending, so some accounts show negative amounts.

Money the government collects from the public or from its own accounts that is subtracted from spending rather than counted as revenue, such as Medicare premiums, rents and royalties from offshore oil leases, and agencies' payments to employee retirement funds.
One of about 20 categories that group federal spending by purpose, regardless of which agency spends it, such as National Defense (050), Health (550), or Social Security (650).
Money the government collects, mostly from taxes, along with customs duties, fees, and earnings sent by the Federal Reserve.
Taxes on wages that fund Social Security (12.4% up to an annual earnings limit) and Medicare's hospital insurance (2.9% on all wages, plus 0.9% on high earners). Workers and employers each pay half.

A federal account that records money dedicated by law to a particular purpose, such as Social Security's retirement fund (OASI) or Medicare's hospital fund (HI). Its reserves are held as special Treasury bonds.
Social Security's two trust funds: Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) pays retirement and survivor benefits, and Disability Insurance (DI) pays disability benefits. OASDI means both combined.
The point at which a trust fund's reserves run out. Benefits wouldn't stop, but by law they could be paid only from incoming taxes, which would cover only part of scheduled benefits.
The total of all wages and self-employment income subject to the Social Security payroll tax. The trustees measure Social Security's shortfall as a percentage of it.
The total value of goods and services produced in the U.S. in a year. Comparing budget figures to GDP shows their size relative to the economy and makes different decades comparable.
A binding commitment to spend money, such as signing a contract or awarding a grant. Outlays happen later when the money is actually paid. USAspending.gov reports award obligations.
The official source for federal spending data by recipient and location, run by the Treasury under the DATA Act. It records grants, contracts, loans, and other financial assistance.

A numbered federal program that gives grants or other aid, such as 93.778 for Medicaid or 20.205 for highway planning and construction. Formerly called the Catalog of Federal Domestic Assistance (CFDA).
A flat amount of income that isn't subject to federal income tax, used by most filers instead of itemizing deductions.
The rate on your last dollar of taxable income. Because the income tax is graduated, your average (effective) rate is lower than your top bracket.
Changes in the economy, such as in work, saving, and investment, caused by a policy, and the feedback of those changes on the budget. Standard cost estimates mostly leave them out.
A label Congress can attach to spending so it doesn't count against budget caps or PAYGO rules. It is used for disaster relief, wars, and pandemic aid.
A tax on imported goods, collected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection from the business importing them.
